lessons.title: Function Creation
lessons.introduction: A function packages a reusable set of instructions under a single descriptive name.
objectives: Write a void function outside setup() and loop().
Identify return type, function name, parameter list, and body.
Avoid duplicating identical blocks of code.
conceptExplanation: You have already used built-in functions like setup(), loop(), and delay(). Creating your own functions lets you name complex behaviors — like stopMotors() or blinkWarning() — so your code stays short, readable, and easy to fix in one place.
lessons.analogy: A function is like a custom button on a microwave labeled 'Popcorn' — instead of manually typing power level and time every time, you press one named action.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Function Creation:
rules: Define your own functions outside setup() and loop().
Use void when the function performs an action without returning a value.

codeExamples.title: Creating a Custom blinkOnce() Function
codeExamples.description: Defines blinkOnce() to flash pin 13 cleanly.

lineByLine.explanation: Declares a custom function that returns nothing (void).

lessons.realWorldApplication: Every clean robotics sketch wraps motor movements (driveForward, turnLeft, stopAll) into named functions.

commonMistakes.fix: Always place function definitions at the top level outside setup() and loop().

tryItYourself.title: m06_func_create.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Call blinkOnce() three times inside setup().
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: The LED flashes cleanly 3 times on startup.

exercises.prompt: What does the keyword void mean before a function name?
options: The function does not return a value.
exercises.explanation: void indicates no return value is sent back to the caller.

summary: Functions group reusable statements under one clear name.
Define functions outside setup() and loop().
Use void when no value is returned.

lessons.title: Function Calls
lessons.introduction: Calling a function jumps execution into its body, runs its instructions, and returns right back to the next line.
objectives: Trace execution order across multiple function calls.
conceptExplanation: Defining a function only teaches the Arduino HOW to do a task — it does not run until you call it by name with parentheses, such as stopMotors();.
lessons.analogy: Writing a recipe in a cookbook doesn't cook dinner; calling the function is actually cooking it.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Function Calls:
rules: Forgetting () when calling a function means it won't execute!
You can call the same function as many times as needed.

codeExamples.title: Calling Multiple Helper Functions
codeExamples.description: Shows clean execution flow from setup() into two helper functions.

lineByLine.explanation: Jumps to printBanner(), prints the banner, then returns.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Startup self-tests call checkBattery(), checkSensors(), and homeServos() in sequence.

commonMistakes.fix: Always include () to invoke a function.

tryItYourself.title: m06_func_call.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Call printBanner() a second time after printReady().
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Prints the banner, then Online, then the banner again.

exercises.prompt: Which line actually invokes a zero-argument function named stopMotors?
exercises.explanation: Parentheses () followed by a semicolon invoke the function.

summary: Functions only run when called.
Always include () when calling a function.
Control returns to the line immediately after the call.

lessons.title: Parameters
lessons.introduction: Parameters let you pass inputs into a function so one function works for many pins, speeds, or durations.
objectives: Declare typed parameters in a function header.
Pass matching arguments when calling the function.
conceptExplanation: Instead of writing blinkPin8(), blinkPin9(), and blinkPin10(), you write one parameterized function blinkPin(int pin, int ms) and pass whichever pin and duration you want.
lessons.analogy: Parameters are like the blank slots on a coffee order: size and drink type change the outcome without needing a separate barista for each drink.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Parameters:
rules: Every parameter must specify its own data type (int pin, int ms — NOT int pin, ms).

codeExamples.title: Parameterized Blink Function
codeExamples.description: Reuses one function to blink two different pins at different speeds.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Traffic light controllers use setLights(bool r, bool y, bool g) to update all 3 LEDs with one clean call.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting the type on the second parameter
commonMistakes.fix: Write (int a, int b), never (int a, b).

tryItYourself.title: m06_parameters.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Add a third call blinkPin(8, 100); inside loop().
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Pin 8 blinks 200 ms, pin 9 blinks 500 ms, then pin 8 blinks quickly for 100 ms.

options: rightSpeed is missing its data type (int rightSpeed).
exercises.explanation: Every parameter in C++ must declare its own type.

summary: Parameters make functions flexible and reusable.
Declare a type for every parameter individually.
Pass arguments in the exact order defined.

lessons.title: Return Values
lessons.introduction: A non-void function computes a result and sends it back to the caller using return.
objectives: Write functions with int, float, or bool return types.
Capture and use returned values in variables or conditions.
conceptExplanation: Functions like analogRead() and millis() hand back a value. You can write your own value-returning functions — such as float readDistanceCm() — so sensor math stays neatly encapsulated.
lessons.analogy: Calling a return-value function is like asking a teammate 'What is the temperature?' and receiving '24.5' back.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Return Values:
rules: The returned value must match the function's declared return type.

codeExamples.title: Returning Voltage from a Helper Function
codeExamples.description: Converts raw ADC counts to volts and returns a float.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Ultrasonic distance meters return distance in cm from measureDistanceCm() so loop() stays clean.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting the return statement in a non-void function
commonMistakes.fix: Always return a value on every code path.

tryItYourself.title: m06_return.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Call adcToVolts(1023) and print it as well.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the keyword that sends the computed value back to the caller.
exercises.explanation: return sends the expression result back to the caller.

summary: Replace void with a data type (int, float, bool) to return a value.
Use return to hand back the computed result.
Capture the returned value in a variable or pass it directly to Serial/if.

lessons.title: Scope
lessons.introduction: Scope defines where a variable is visible and how long it lives in memory: global vs local variables.
objectives: Differentiate global variables from local variables.
Explain why local variables reset on every function call unless declared static.
conceptExplanation: A variable declared inside { } (like inside setup() or a for loop) is LOCAL — only code inside those braces can see it, and it disappears when the block ends. A variable declared outside all functions is GLOBAL and persists across loop() cycles.
lessons.analogy: Global variables are on a shared office whiteboard; local variables are on your personal notepad at your desk.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Scope:
rules: Never accidentally shadow a global variable by declaring a local variable with the exact same name.
Use local variables for temporary calculations; use global (or static) variables for state that must survive between loop() cycles.

codeExamples.title: Global State vs Local Scratch Variable
codeExamples.description: Tracks persistent count globally while keeping sensor reading local.

lineByLine.explanation: Global: remembers its value across loop() iterations.

lessons.realWorldApplication: State machines (like button toggle state or previous millis() timestamp) must be global or static so they don't reset to 0 every millisecond.

commonMistakes.mistake: Declaring unsigned long prevMillis = 0; as a plain local inside loop()
commonMistakes.fix: It resets to 0 every pass! Declare it global or 'static unsigned long prevMillis = 0;'.

tryItYourself.title: m06_scope.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Observe why pressCount keeps growing while localStep stays 1.

exercises.prompt: What happens if you declare `int count = 0;` as a non-static local variable inside loop()?
options: It resets back to 0 every time loop() restarts.
exercises.explanation: Non-static local variables are recreated fresh on every entry to loop().

summary: Local variables live only inside their { } block.
Global variables persist across loop() cycles.
Use local variables for temporary math and global/static for persistent state.

lessons.title: Reusable Functions
lessons.introduction: Reusable functions avoid hardcoded pins and magic numbers so you can drop them straight into future robotics projects.
objectives: Pass pin numbers and thresholds as parameters.
conceptExplanation: A function hardcoded to pin 9 only works on one circuit. A reusable function accepts the pin and threshold as parameters, making it a building block you can reuse across Uno, Nano, Mega, and ESP32 projects.
lessons.analogy: A reusable function is like a standard USB-C charger — it works across many devices instead of being glued to one gadget.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Reusable Functions:
rules: Accept pins and sample counts as parameters.
Use long for sums so adding multiple 10-bit readings never overflows int.

codeExamples.title: Reusable Sensor Smoothing Function
codeExamples.description: Averages N analog samples on any analog pin to reduce noise.

lineByLine.explanation: Prevents 16-bit int overflow when summing many readings.
Works on any analog pin with any sample count.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Noisy light, soil, and IR distance sensors become dramatically steadier when wrapped in a reusable averaging function.

commonMistakes.mistake: Summing 50 analogRead() values into a 16-bit int
commonMistakes.fix: 50 * 1023 = 51,150 which overflows 16-bit int (32,767)! Use long for sums.

tryItYourself.title: m06_reusable.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change the sample count from 10 to 20 in loop().
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Prints a smoother 20-sample average of A0 every 300 ms.

exercises.prompt: Why did readAverageAdc use `long sum` instead of `int sum` on Uno R3?
options: Summing many 0–1023 readings can exceed 16-bit int max (32,767).
int cannot be added in a for loop.
exercises.explanation: 33 samples of 1023 already exceed 32,767; long avoids overflow.

summary: Parameterize pins and counts to make functions reusable.
Use long accumulators when summing multiple ADC readings.
Build your own personal toolbox of tested helper functions.

lessons.title: Modular Programming
lessons.introduction: Modular programming organizes a complex robotics program into clean, cohesive functions where loop() reads like a high-level story.
objectives: Structure loop() as a sequence of clean function calls.
Separate sensing, decision making, and actuation cleanly.
conceptExplanation: When a sketch grows past 40 lines, putting everything inside loop() turns debugging into a nightmare. Modular programming keeps loop() to 5–10 readable lines that call well-named helper functions.
lessons.analogy: A conductor doesn't play every instrument — the conductor signals the strings, brass, and percussion modules at the right moments.

syntaxExplanation.summary: Core C++ syntax pattern for Modular Programming:
rules: Each function should do one clear job and fit on one screen.
Name functions with active verbs: readSensor(), updateDisplay(), stopMotors().

codeExamples.title: Modular Autonomous Loop
codeExamples.description: Demonstrates how readable loop() becomes when decomposed into modular helpers.

lineByLine.explanation: loop() reads like plain English without low-level pin clutter.

lessons.realWorldApplication: Modular sketches let you swap a motor driver or ultrasonic sensor later by editing just one function instead of rewriting the whole program.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a 200-line loop() with no helper functions
commonMistakes.fix: Extract distinct tasks into small named functions as soon as loop() grows past ~20 lines.

tryItYourself.title: m06_modular.ino
tryItYourself.challengePrompt: Change mockDistance() to return 35.0f and verify the output switches to 'Driving forward'.
tryItYourself.expectedBehavior: Prints 'Driving forward' every second when mockDistance() returns 35.0f.

exercises.prompt: What is the hallmark of well-written modular Arduino code?
options: loop() is short and readable, delegating sensing and actuation to focused helper functions.
All code is placed on a single line.
exercises.explanation: Modular design keeps high-level logic clear and isolates low-level hardware details.

summary: Modular programming splits logic into focused, single-purpose functions.
Keep loop() concise and readable like a high-level summary.
Isolating hardware details makes upgrading sensors or motors easy.
